It argues that big business, being interstate, belongs under federal oversight, rattling Wall Street, and draws more comment for being printed in simplified spelling. He receives Mabel Boardman and about 100 Red Cross delegates and later hears the Boston Symphony with Edith.

headline: Mark Twain to lunch; three new monuments
summary: Roosevelt proclaims El Morro, Montezuma Castle and Petrified Forest as national monuments. Mark Twain, John Philip Sousa and Admiral Dewey are among the day's callers, and Twain stays for lunch. Harriman calls at six, and Roosevelt finishes the night at the Gridiron Dinner.

headline: Nobel Peace Prize awarded
summary: In Christiania, Norway, Roosevelt is formally awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for ending the Russo-Japanese War, the first American so honored. He wires thanks to the Nobel committee, pledging the prize money to a permanent body for industrial peace. That night he and Edith go to the Columbia Theater.

headline: Retreat on simplified spelling
summary: Under heavy pressure, Roosevelt withdraws his order telling the Public Printer to use simplified spelling. Two houseguests, Beekman Winthrop and Paul Morton, are staying at the White House, and the Cabinet comes to dinner. He writes Hitchcock about illegal fences on public land and federal coal lands.

headline: Buffalo Bill and a medal for Peary

His brother-in-law Douglas Robinson is a houseguest.

headline: Moody to the Supreme Court; a Cabinet shuffle
summary: Roosevelt puts Moody on the Supreme Court, moves Bonaparte from Navy to Attorney General, shifts Metcalf to Navy and names Oscar Straus to Commerce and Labor. He sends Congress special messages on naval personnel and public land laws, and one on the canal illustrated with Canal Zone photographs.
